issues.legal_issue: A co-owner may validly participate in a lease made by the other co-owners to a concern of which that co-owner is a proprietor.
material_facts: Several co-owners leased property to a business that was then the sole proprietorship of one of the co-owners.
The lease was challenged as invalid because one co-owner was on both sides of the transaction.
issues.conclusion: The lease was not invalid merely because one co-owner participated on both sides of the transaction.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, contemplates transfers by a person to himself and one or more other persons. The Court distinguished Girish Chandra v. Srinath and Rye v. Rye, [1962] A.C. 496, and held that a contract between a person and himself together with others is not for that reason invalid.

predicates.co_owners_lease_to_concern_of_one_coowne: Several co-owners leased property to a concern of which one of them was a proprietor.

issues.definition: When several co-owners lease property to a concern of which one is a proprietor, the lease is not invalid merely because that co-owner participated on both sides.

issues.legal_issue: A conveyance of leased land does not transfer a tenant-built superstructure when the conveyance terms exclude that superstructure.
material_facts: The tenants had taken the land on lease and constructed the superstructure on it.
The terms of the conveyance to the purchaser did not include the tenants’ superstructure.
The superstructure remained on the land while the lease subsisted.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser acquired the land but not the superstructure, which remained the tenants’ property while the lease subsisted.
issues.legal_principle: The Court construed the lease and conveyance documents and concluded that the superstructures built by the lessees were not included in the property conveyed. It also rejected the contention that the lease was invalid merely because one co-owner was among the lessees, applying section 5 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.

predicates.civil_property_title_dispute: A civil property dispute concerns whether a purchaser acquired a superstructure standing on leased land.
predicates.tenant_built_superstructure: The tenant constructed the superstructure on the leased land.
predicates.conveyance_terms_exclude_superstructure: The conveyance terms did not include the tenant-built superstructure.

issues.definition: In a civil property title dispute, if the tenant built the superstructure and the conveyance excluded it, the purchaser did not acquire title to that superstructure.

issues.legal_issue: A rent-control authority’s consideration of a claimant’s landlord status does not confer jurisdiction to finally decide title to immovable property.
material_facts: The landlord sought fixation of fair rent under the rent-control legislation.
The tenants disputed the landlord’s title and claimed ownership of the superstructure.

The rent-control authority had to consider whether the applicant was a landlord, but its statutory function was to decide rent-related relief and its jurisdiction on landlord status was limited and prima facie.
The legislation did not expressly exclude the civil court’s jurisdiction over title disputes.
issues.conclusion: The rent-control authority could consider landlord status only for the limited purpose of exercising its jurisdiction and could not finally determine title to the property.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4, 10(1) and its proviso, and 10(2)(vii) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, show that the authority’s role is limited; section 19 does not extend finality to a title determination in a fair-rent proceeding. Under section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, civil-court jurisdiction is not curtailed without clear statutory warrant. The Court relied on Dhulabhai v. State, [1968] 3 SCR 662; Mathura Prasad Bajoo Jaiswal v. Dossibai N.B. Jeejeebhoy, [1970] 3 SCR 830; Gangabai v. Chhabubai, [1982] 1 SCR 1176; Jeeth Kaur v. Smt. P. Kondalamma, AIR 1983 AP 219; and State of Tamil Nadu v. Ramalinga Samigal Madam, [1985] 4 SCC 10, among other authorities.

predicates.rent_control_proceeding: A proceeding is brought before a rent-control authority for relief concerning rent or eviction.
predicates.landlord_status_is_jurisdictional_thresh: The authority must consider whether the applicant is a landlord to determine whether it may hear the proceeding.
predicates.statutory_scheme_limits_authority_to_ren: The governing scheme limits the authority to rent-related relief and does not authorize it to finally determine ownership.

issues.definition: In a rent-control proceeding, if landlord status is only a jurisdictional threshold and the scheme limits the authority to rent-related relief, the authority cannot finally adjudicate title.

issues.legal_issue: A final finding on title made incidentally in a rent-control proceeding does not bar a civil court from deciding title when it is directly in issue in a later civil suit.
material_facts: In an earlier fair-rent proceeding, the rent-control appellate authority decided that the landlord owned the property and fixed fair rent.
The earlier title determination was made while deciding a rent-control application, not as the direct issue in an ordinary civil suit.
A later civil suit sought recovery of rent and required determination of whether the claimant owned the property and was entitled to recover rent.
issues.conclusion: The earlier rent-control finding did not preclude the civil court from examining title; the civil court could decide that issue independently.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that title is not directly and substantially determined by a rent-control authority of limited jurisdiction when it is considered only incidentally to a rent-control remedy. Section 19 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, does not extend to an application under section 4. The Court relied on section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and its Explanation VIII, while applying the principles in Dhulabhai v. State, [1968] 3 SCR 662; Mathura Prasad Bajoo Jaiswal v. Dossibai N.B. Jeejeebhoy, [1970] 3 SCR 830; Gangabai v. Chhabubai, [1982] 1 SCR 1176; and Jeeth Kaur v. Smt. P. Kondalamma, AIR 1983 AP 219.

predicates.later_civil_suit_directly_puts_title_in_: A later ordinary civil suit directly requires a decision on ownership or entitlement to recover rent.
predicates.prior_rent_control_title_finding_was_inc: A rent-control authority considered title only while deciding an application for rent-control relief.

issues.definition: If a later civil suit directly puts title in issue and the earlier rent-control title finding was incidental, the civil court may decide title independently.

issues.legal_issue: A civil court may not redetermine the fair rent fixed by the rent-control authority when deciding a civil claim for rent, provided the landlord-tenant relationship and entitlement to recover are established.
material_facts: The rent-control authority fixed fair rent for the premises.
The claimant later sought recovery of rent in a civil suit on the basis of that fair-rent determination.
The Court explained that, if the civil court found the landlord-tenant relationship and the claimant’s entitlement to recover rent, it would have to use the fair rent fixed by the authority.
issues.conclusion: The civil court must apply the fair rent fixed by the rent-control authority and may not redetermine its amount.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, assigns determination of fair rent to the rent-control authority; that determination is exclusively within its jurisdiction and is impliedly excluded from civil-court jurisdiction. The Court also referred to Raval & Co. v. Ramachandran, [1974] 1 SCC 424, on applications for fair rent by a landlord or tenant.

predicates.civil_rent_recovery_suit: A civil suit seeks recovery of rent on the basis of a rent-control determination.
predicates.rent_control_authority_fixed_fair_rent: The rent-control authority fixed fair rent for the premises.
predicates.landlord_tenant_relationship_and_recover: The civil court finds that the parties have a landlord-tenant relationship and that the claimant is entitled to recover rent.

issues.definition: If a civil rent-recovery suit relies on fair rent fixed by the rent-control authority and the claimant’s recovery entitlement is established, the civil court must apply that fixed rent without redetermining it.
